claims.text: Crystalline near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles containing five or more metals face a risk of structural or chemical instability in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime.
Introducing a thin inert oxide shell can overcome this instability risk.
The oxide shell prevents diffusion of reactive species.
The oxide shell reduces nanoparticle exposure to the reactive environment.
Reduced reactive-species diffusion and environmental exposure preserve nanoparticle structural stability.
Reduced reactive-species diffusion and environmental exposure preserve nanoparticle chemical stability.
Oxide-shelled nanoparticles will be more stable than otherwise identical nanoparticles without the shell.
Oxide-shelled nanoparticles will retain catalytic activity for longer than otherwise identical unshelled nanoparticles.
The proposed stabilization applies throughout 773–1173 K.
The proposed stabilization applies for thermal exposures lasting several hours to days.
The hypothesis is scoped to near-equiatomic solid solutions of five or more metals.
Shell effectiveness may depend on shell thickness, composition, and uniformity.
Shell effectiveness may depend on the reactive environment and operating conditions.
Significant degradation of activity or structural or chemical stability in the shelled nanoparticles after exposure would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction is relative improvement over an unshelled control, whereas the failure rule uses absolute 'significant degradation' in the shelled sample. A shelled sample could degrade significantly yet still outperform the control, so the stated rule could reject an outcome consistent with the prediction.
